nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What methodology was used to collect data in the study?
nodes.answer: A concurrent triangulation methodology of teaching and learning was employed, including teacher ethnographic accounts, student self-assessments, and STEM researchers' observations.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract This study breaks new ground in educational theory by empirically validating how artificial intelligence (AI) competencies emerge through social learning ecosystems in underserved communities. Through an innovative cross-national mixed-methods design, we examined 330 secondary school students across the UK, Greece, and Bra- zil who developed AI competencies while addressing Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through open schooling initiatives. Our theoretical innovation synthesises UNESCO S AI Competencies Framework with the CARE-KNOW-DO pedagogi- cal model, generating transformative insights into AI literacy. We conceptualise Al literacy as a dynamic interplay of understanding, applying, and creating AI through social practice, where learners develop ethical awareness (CARE), epistemic-technical competence (KNOW), and responsible agency (DO) within authentic learning ecosys- items. Employing a concurrent triangulation methodology of teaching and learning, we collected comprehensive longitudinal data through teacher ethnographic accounts, student self-assessments, STEM researchers observations and granular analysis of Al-enabled project work over a year. This robust methodological approach revealed seven dimensions of Al-supported competency linked to transversal skills develop- ment across three distinct but interrelated domains. CARE (Understanding Al) high- lights how proactive exploration and affective engagement emerge socially.

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What is the teaching model proposed in the project?
nodes.answer: The teaching model proposed is the socioscientific inquiry-based learning model (SSIBL).
nodes.paragraph: This project proposed a teaching and training model named the socioscientific inquiry-based learning model (SSIBL), grounded on three teaching concepts socio- scientific issues (SSIs), inquiry-based science education, and civic literacy education. In this model, SSIs, as the learning context, usually refer to Anthropocene challenges, which include the dilemma between scientific and technical development and societal change. Thus, infusing SSIs into the classroom is envisaged as a crucial aspect of future science education if it is to equip students with the competencies to respond to the vari- ous challenges they will meet in an uncertain future. SSI-based teaching and learning have demonstrated a variety of positive effects on students science learning, including science content (Badeo & Duque, 2022), decision- making (Authors, 2021), environmental NOS views (Herman, 2018), and moral sensi- tivity (Fowler et al., 2009), etc. However, the integration of SSI into science education presents several challenges. According to Zeidler et al. (2019), SSI education should ideally engage students in controversial and ill-structured problems that require interdis- ciplinary thinking and evidence-based reasoning.
